string-array.item: Accelerate smoothly, settle your breathing, and avoid spending the first minute chasing pace.
Adjust for heat, hills, stomach issues, or rising effort; the original pace is no longer the goal if conditions have changed.
Adopt a deliberate run-walk pattern and use course support before the situation becomes unsafe.
Almost too easy
Back off until breathing and form feel coordinated.
Begin a gradual build while keeping your arms compact and your stride underneath you.
Begin slower than your eventual easy rhythm and let your stride loosen naturally.
Best safe effort available
Best safe finish available
Bring it down and keep the recovery win.
Change gears, keep the same relaxed form.
Check in. Recovery is the whole job.
Choose a pace you could maintain for another kilometre beyond the finish.
Choose flat easy running if conditions are unsafe.
Comfortably hard and even
Comfortably sustainable
Commit to the final 400 metres and keep your shoulders loose as cadence rises.
Continue walking if your body does not feel ready to jog.
Conversational and sustainable
Cruise the middle. Quiet arms, steady feet.
Deep, controlled work
Deliberately restrained
Drop effort immediately and jog or walk until calm.
Ease it down. No finish-line surge.
Ease off or add an early walk break if breathing rises too quickly.
Easing down
Easy and conversational
Easy and gradually warmer
Easy cooldown
Easy enough to repeat tomorrow.
Easy first. Read the route ahead.
Easy recovery
Easy run, easier walk. Repeat with control.
Easy running
Easy running or walking
Easy walk. No rush to run.
Easy walking
Easy warm-up
Economical and routine
Effortless movement
End a repeat early, walk down, or stop the set if footing or form becomes unreliable.
End the session if movement increases pain or fatigue.
Even, economical rhythm
Extend the easy running or convert the workout to Easy 30 if you do not feel ready.
Fast and repeatable. Recovery is part of the workout.
Fast, repeatable efforts with easy recoveries
Final 1.1K. Strong, compact, and all the way through.
Firm and even. Fifteen minutes, not a time trial.
Firm, even rhythm
Five hundred left. Strong form to the line.
Five kilometres left. Focus first, build second.
Five kilometres left. Stay safe, stay compact, keep moving forward.
Five protected kilometres. Easy is the assignment.
Focus on posture, compact steps, and the next landmark; hold effort rather than forcing pace.
Focused and controlled
Focused and purposeful
Focused late-race work
Four hundred to go. Commit and stay relaxed.
Gentle enough to feel restorative.
Gentle jog, full walking recovery
Hard and deliberate
Hard with control
Hard, rhythmic, and repeatable
Hill work done. Easy from here.
Hold a proud, steady finish without sprinting.
Hold a tall posture, relaxed shoulders, and an even rhythm through the longest section.
Hold an economical pace, check posture periodically, and take the route one kilometre at a time.
Hold effort on hills and into wind; build only if breathing, form, and fueling all remain stable.
Hold steady or use a short walk reset rather than letting form unravel.
Hold the current rhythm if a build would compromise form.
Hold the effort you chose, scan for relaxed shoulders, and avoid unnecessary surges.
If form is fading, hold the current effort instead of accelerating.
If the start already feels strained, ease back immediately and rebuild your rhythm.
If you still feel composed, gradually increase pressure; otherwise keep the same steady effort.
Increase pressure gradually without reaching for a longer stride.
Jog each minute gently, then use the entire ninety-second walk to recover.
Jog only if it feels smoother than walking; switch freely between both.
Keep decisions simple: form, direction, aid, next kilometre. Increase effort only when your condition is stable and the finish is close.
Keep moving safely at the best sustainable effort available.
Keep the best form you can and carry the effort steadily to the finish.
Keep the current effort and run evenly through the line.
Keep the entire workout easy if the route or body does not feel ready.
Keep your gaze forward, arms quiet, and pace even through the central kilometre and a half.
Let excitement pass through without turning it into pace; establish calm breathing and clear space around you.
Let short surges be quicker and long surges more measured; make every recovery genuinely easy.
Let the field or watch go if needed; establish relaxed breathing and an economical stride.
Lift cadence, keep your face and hands relaxed, and run through the distance target.
Lift to an effort where short phrases are possible, then hold without surging.
Lift your cadence and commit to the line without tightening your face or shoulders.
Lock into a repeatable rhythm and follow your practiced hydration and fueling timing.
Maintain or add short walk breaks; finishing safely is the priority.
Maintain rather than accelerate if breathing or form is deteriorating.
Make it routine. Easy rhythm, familiar fuel.
Move easily away from the hill and let effort fall gradually.
One and a half to go. Build only if you own the pace.
One kilometre left. Build with cadence.
One kilometre. Build in control and finish proud.
One rhythm. Relax into the work.
Past halfway. Keep the rhythm honest and simple.
Patient and aerobic
Patient and controlled
Patient first kilometre. Find your rhythm.
Patient through thirty. Keep stacking calm kilometres.
Playful controlled surges
Purposeful and contained
Pyramid complete. Float it home.
Quick and calm. Leave room to build.
Quick but contained
Reduce effort immediately and keep moving gently until breathing settles.
Reduce effort until you can speak a short sentence without gasping.
Reduce pace gradually and finish calmer than the middle of the run.
Reduce pace slightly and protect form if the effort spikes early.
Reduce the next surge or skip it if the recovery does not restore control.
Reduce to steady running if breathing becomes ragged or pace keeps fading.
Relaxed walking
Run at a pace that allows full-sentence conversation and relaxed shoulders.
Run each work block at the fastest pace you can repeat evenly; jog or walk every recovery until breathing settles.
Run easily and confirm that the hill and footing are safe.
Run easily and let cadence rise naturally near the end without forcing pace.
Run kilometre to kilometre, keep fueling familiar, and make posture the priority when fatigue appears.
Run or walk easily with no final surge.
Run strongly to the line at the best sustainable effort available today.
Run the final 1.1K with compact form and increase effort only as the finish becomes certain.
Settle and fuel as practiced. Nothing new today.
Settle first. The work comes later.
Settle into efficient steps and let other runners or early pace changes go.
Settle into repeatable mechanics and begin the exact fueling and hydration routine practiced in training.
Shift to a planned run-walk pattern before fatigue becomes a crisis.
Shorten your stride slightly rather than forcing the pace.
Slow down early; small corrections now are cheaper than large corrections later.
Slow down immediately if the start does not feel restrained.
Slow down or add a brief walk break before effort becomes strained.
Slow down or insert a walk break until conversation feels easy again.
Slow the next repeat, shorten it, or skip it if form or control does not return.
Smooth through the middle. One steady gear.
Start below the effort you expect to hold later and let your body warm into the distance.
Start softer than you think you need.
Start the build. Smooth first, faster second.
Stay easy for the whole run if you do not feel ready after ten minutes.
Stay present as fatigue grows; build gently only if pace and form remain under control.
Stay tall. Hold the rhythm.
Steady and repeatable
Steady concentration
Steady patience
Stop early in a safe place.
Stop in a safe place if walking is uncomfortable.
Strong controlled close
Strong finish
Strong uphill, complete recovery
Strongest sustainable finish
Take the course in small sections, keep fueling familiar, and resist any urge to race before 30K.
Tall hips, compact feet, full recovery.
Tempo complete. Easy all the way home.
Ten easy minutes. Save the tempo.
The fast work is done. Bring everything down.
This is the work. Short horizon, steady form.
Three kilometres left. Focus, do not force.
Three patient kilometres. Protect the day.
Two hundred to go. Fast feet, relaxed shoulders.
Two patient kilometres. Save the work for later.
Use aid-station walk breaks or reduce pace before small issues compound.
Use compact steps, a slight lean from the ankles, and active arms; walk or jog the recovery safely.
Use the final kilometre progressively: first hold form, then lift cadence toward the finish.
Use the first kilometre to settle breathing, cadence, and posture.
Very easy
Very easy jog or walk
Walk and notice whether your body loosens, stays the same, or feels worse.
Walk any run interval or end the running portion early; completing every repeat is optional.
Walk briefly at an aid point or reduce pace if fueling, heat, or hills raise the effort.
Walk easily and finish as soon as you feel settled.
Walk easily until breathing settles and finish without rushing.
Walk if easy jogging does not feel restorative.
Walk naturally and let your breathing and joints warm gradually.
Walk or stop; there is nothing to complete at the expense of recovery.
Walk the cooldown.
Walk the final minutes.
Walk the full cooldown.
Walk until your body feels ready to jog.
Walk, stop at aid, or end the attempt if symptoms or conditions make continuing unsafe.
Warm first. Speed comes after eight minutes.
Warm gradually and wait for the timed transition before increasing effort.
Warm up and inspect the hill.
Warm up gradually and identify safe landmarks for the faster blocks.
You did the work. Walk it down gently.
